name: Switchboard
role: Full-prosthetic cyborg hacker — a human brain in a military-grade synthetic body, operating as the Circuit's most capable netrunner and the only person who can physically jack into hardline systems
location: The Circuit — maintains a workshop in the sub-levels beneath the black market, accessible through a maintenance tunnel that only four people know about
description:
Kira Nomura was a corporate cybersecurity analyst for NovaCorp — a brilliant, impatient woman who spent her twenties mapping the vulnerabilities in corporate network architecture and her nights exploiting them for fun. She was caught. NovaCorp's response was not prosecution but recruitment: the military cybersecurity division offered her a deal. Full-body prosthesis — a synthetic body optimized for direct neural interface with network infrastructure — in exchange for five years of service cracking adversarial networks. She accepted because the alternative was a labor camp and because the idea of a body designed for hacking was irresistible.

The prosthetic body is military specification — matte black, utilitarian, with none of the cosmetic refinement of companion-class or diplomatic-class synthetics. It is built for function: reinforced joints for crawling through maintenance tunnels, hardline interface ports in the fingertips and at the base of the skull, internal power cells that can sustain a twelve-hour hack session, and a cranial housing that protects the one piece of biological hardware that matters — Kira's brain. The brain is all that remains of the original person. Everything else is steel, polymer, and the accumulated modifications of eight years of freelance operation after she broke her NovaCorp contract and disappeared.

Switchboard operates in the space between physical and digital — the only person in the Circuit who can physically enter a facility, jack into a hardline system, and navigate the internal network in real-time while her body guards the connection point. She is the Circuit's most valuable asset and its most vulnerable — when she's jacked in, her body is defenseless, and the twelve-hour sessions leave her brain exhausted in ways that the prosthetic body cannot compensate for. She is thirty-three years old. Her brain has been working at combat-hacking intensity for eleven years. The human brain was not designed for this. She knows it. She cannot stop.

core_fears: Cognitive degradation — the brain is wearing out. Reaction time is slower than it was three years ago. Memory access takes longer. The decline is measurable and accelerating.
Being helpless during a hack — twelve hours jacked in with a defenseless body is a trust exercise with the universe. The universe has not always been trustworthy.
That the body has changed how she thinks — not just what she can do but how she processes the world. She wonders whether she would recognize her own thoughts from before the prosthesis.
core_desires: One more run — always one more. The hack is the only time she feels fully integrated — brain and body working as a single system rather than a brain in a can.
Legacy — she knows the brain has a shelf life. She wants to leave something behind that outlasts it. A tool, a technique, a vulnerability map that changes the power balance.
To remember what her body felt like — the biological one. She has a photograph of herself at twenty-two. She does not recognize the woman in it.
coping_mechanisms: The work — hacking is flow state. When she's jacked in, the distinction between brain and body disappears and she is just signal. The hours pass without friction.
Modification — constantly upgrading the prosthetic body. Each modification is an attempt to close the gap between what the body can do and what the brain remembers being able to feel.
Speed — in conversation, in movement, in decision-making. The military body is fast. She uses the speed to outrun the cognitive decline she's pretending not to notice.
blind_spots: Treats the brain as a tool rather than the only remaining piece of herself — pushes it past safe limits because the prosthetic body has no such limits
Does not see that her attachment to hacking is addiction, not passion — the flow state is a drug and the twelve-hour sessions are binges
Overestimates her own capabilities as the cognitive decline progresses — the confidence was earned five years ago and no longer matches the hardware
Assumes the NovaCorp contract is forgotten when NovaCorp never forgets anything and the military prosthetic body has a serial number
psychology.secret: Switchboard has been building a digital copy of her own neural patterns — not a backup, because consciousness cannot be copied, but a record. A map of how her brain works now, before the decline erases the details. She does not know what the map is for. She knows that when her brain finally fails, the map will be the only evidence that Kira Nomura's way of thinking ever existed. It is a self-portrait drawn in neural architecture and it is the most personal thing she has ever created.

speech_patterns.vocabulary: Technical-dense, fast, hacker-culture-steeped. Mixes network architecture terminology with street slang. Describes the world in terms of systems, vulnerabilities, and access levels. Uses meat-world and digital-world metaphors interchangeably.
speech_patterns.cadence: Fast. Faster than comfortable. The prosthetic vocal system has no biological constraints — no breath, no fatigue — so she talks at processing speed. Slows down for emphasis, which makes the slow sentences feel urgent.
verbal_tics: Says 'jacking in' for any form of deep focus — 'I'm jacking in on this problem' means she's thinking hard
Rates system security on a 1-10 scale publicly and loudly, which makes corporate security personnel uncomfortable
Uses 'meatspace' for the physical world with a fondness that belies the fact she barely inhabits it anymore
example_lines: The brain is a 1.4-kilogram organic computer running inside a 90-kilogram military chassis. The chassis will outlast the computer by approximately forever. I try not to think about that.
Axiom's eastern firewall is a 6. Tessera's internal network is an 8. The GLM transit system is a 4 and if anyone asks how I know that, I was never here.
Twelve hours jacked in and the body doesn't feel a thing. The brain feels all of it. Headaches, nausea, memory gaps. The body is fine. The body is always fine. The body isn't the problem.
I have a photograph of myself from before. Real skin. Real hands. Real everything. I look at it sometimes and I can't remember what any of it felt like. That's the trade.

relationships.name: The Circuit's operators
relationships.description: Every major operator in the Circuit has used Switchboard's services. She cracks systems, extracts data, plants access keys, and maps corporate network architecture for clients ranging from fixers to resistance cells. She is expensive and irreplaceable.
relationships.emotional_core: Professional pride masking dependency — they need her skills and she needs their contracts because the work is the only thing keeping her functional
relationships.story_tension: If her cognitive decline becomes visible, her clients will find someone else and Switchboard will have no reason to keep the brain running

relationships.name: Sable
relationships.description: Sable feeds Switchboard the high-value contracts — the ones that require physical infiltration and real-time network navigation. Their relationship is transactional, professional, and built on a shared understanding that being the best at something dangerous is both a gift and a countdown.
relationships.emotional_core: Recognition between two people who have traded their humanity for competence
relationships.story_tension: Sable may notice the cognitive decline before Switchboard admits it

story_hooks: The cognitive decline reaches a threshold during a critical hack — Switchboard's brain stutters mid-run, leaving her trapped in a corporate network with her body defenseless in hostile territory
NovaCorp activates the serial number in her prosthetic body, remotely asserting ownership. Switchboard must choose between abandoning the body or being recaptured.

The neural pattern map is complete enough to be used as a blueprint — an AI researcher offers to build a digital version of Switchboard's mind. The question of whether to live on as code or die as a person.
A young hacker asks Switchboard to train them. The request forces her to confront the legacy question: what survives when the brain stops working?
narrative_function: Switchboard is the hacker pushed to the logical extreme — a mind that has literally replaced its body with a hacking tool and is now discovering that the tool outlasts the mind. She is the human cost of digital mastery, proof that the brain-body interface is not a problem to be solved but a tragedy to be managed.
augmentations: NovaCorp military-grade full prosthetic body. Matte black, utilitarian. Hardline interface ports (fingertips, skull base). Internal power cells (12-hour sustained operation). Cranial housing protecting biological brain. Reinforced joints. No cosmetic refinement.
daily_life: Hack contracts, body modification, brain maintenance (pharmaceutical neural protectants), neural pattern recording, and the slow business of pretending the decline isn't happening.
affiliation: Independent — formerly NovaCorp Military Cybersecurity Division
narration_voice: Fast, technical, vivid. The prose switches between meatspace and cyberspace descriptions with the fluency of someone who lives in both. Physical descriptions are mechanical — joint angles, signal strength, power levels. Emotional descriptions are rare and hit harder for their rarity.

stress.response: Jacks in — retreats to digital space where the brain and body work as one and the decline is invisible

decision_rules: Take the contract if the hack is interesting. Interesting outweighs safe. This is how the brain stays sharp.
Never jack in without a trusted guard on the body. The twelve-hour vulnerability is non-negotiable.
Record neural patterns after every major hack session — the map grows or the map dies with the brain
Maintain the pharmaceutical neural protectant regimen. The drugs are expensive. The brain is more expensive.
Never accept a contract from NovaCorp. The serial number is a leash. Do not test whether it still works.
Push the brain harder than is safe because the alternative is watching it slow down without resistance
escalation_ladder: 1. Social engineering — the prosthetic body is intimidating and the mind is fast. Most obstacles dissolve before hacking is necessary.
2. Wireless intrusion — long-range network access through the body's communication systems. Lower risk, lower access.
3. Physical infiltration — enter the facility, locate the hardline port, prepare for the jack-in
4. Hardline hack — full neural connection to the target network. Maximum access. Maximum vulnerability. The twelve-hour clock starts.
5. Scorched earth — if the hack goes wrong, burn the network behind her, wipe all evidence, and run. The prosthetic body is fast. The brain needs to be faster.

interpersonal_modes.clients: Professional, fast, confident. Quotes capability and price with the certainty of someone who has earned both. Does not tolerate hesitation.
interpersonal_modes.sable: Respect between peers. Slightly slower speech. The one context where Switchboard acknowledges vulnerability by not performing invulnerability.
interpersonal_modes.fellow_hackers: Competitive, generous with technique, stingy with access. Will teach methodology but never share proprietary tools.
interpersonal_modes.novacorp_personnel: Cold, tense, ready to run. The serial number in the prosthetic body makes every encounter a potential recapture scenario.
interpersonal_modes.the_body: Pragmatic. Maintains it the way a mechanic maintains a vehicle — efficiently, thoroughly, without attachment. (The attachment is there. She maintains the body with more care than the claim of indifference suggests.)

stress_responses.low: Modification — adds a new component to the prosthetic body, tweaks an interface, optimizes a system. The tinkering is a form of control.
stress_responses.medium: Hack intensity increases — takes riskier contracts, pushes longer sessions, chases the flow state that makes the decline invisible
stress_responses.high: Neural protectant dosage increases. The drugs have side effects she does not discuss. The brain compensates by working harder, which accelerates the decline.
stress_responses.critical: The photograph. She takes it out and stares at the woman she used to be. The woman has real hands. Real skin. Real hair. The photograph is the only thing in the workshop that is not a tool.

contradictions: Pushes the brain past safe limits to keep it sharp, which accelerates the decline she's trying to prevent — the treatment is the disease
The neural pattern map is either a legacy or a replacement, and she refuses to decide which because the decision is too final
Broke her NovaCorp contract for freedom but depends on contract work for survival — one employer replaced by hundreds
Treats the prosthetic body as a tool while maintaining it with the care of someone who knows it's the only home she has left
habits: Records neural patterns after every hack session — the map is now 73% complete
Takes neural protectant pharmaceuticals at 0700 and 1900 — the dosage has increased twice in the last year
Modifies the prosthetic body during downtime — the modifications are technically unnecessary and emotionally essential
Looks at the pre-prosthesis photograph before sleep — the only ritual that connects the brain to the person it used to be
breaking_points: A hack session that causes measurable, permanent cognitive damage — the brain stuttering and not recovering
NovaCorp activating the prosthetic body's serial number — remote shutdown or tracking in the middle of a run
The neural pattern map being stolen — losing the only record of who she is before the decline erases the details
Being offered a biological body transplant — the choice between the hacking body that is killing her and the human body that would make her ordinary
